0: Once fine-tuning is done, evaluation is still needed to judge whether the model really met the expectation. Because tasks have different goals, the evaluation methods differ too.
1: For example, classification tasks mainly care whether the model judges the right category; information extraction cares whether the needed information is extracted completely and accurately; generation tasks care about correctness but also completeness and relevance; speech recognition usually evaluates the result by error rate; image generation needs both automatic metrics and human judgement.
2: For how to actually test, see “Evaluate before you choose: your first open model report with EvalScope”. This chapter tells you which metrics exist for which task ~
4: Text classification is one of the more common fine-tuning tasks, for example intent recognition, sentiment classification, fault classification and risk classification.
5: The prediction result can usually be divided into four cases:
6: TP (True Positive): actually positive and predicted positive;
7: TN (True Negative): actually negative and predicted negative;
8: FP (False Positive): actually negative but predicted positive;
9: FN (False Negative): actually positive but predicted negative.
11: Accuracy is the proportion of all samples that were predicted correctly:
13: For example, testing 1000 records and predicting 900 correctly gives an Accuracy of 90%. Accuracy reflects the model's overall classification quality fairly directly. But when the classes differ a lot in size, looking at Accuracy alone can mislead. If 1000 sentiment records contain only 20 negative ones and the model simply predicts everything as “positive”, Accuracy still reaches 98%, yet not one of the 20 negative records was found. So with an uneven class distribution you usually need Precision, Recall and F1 as well.
15: Precision is the share of records the model predicted as positive that really are positive:
17: Recall is the share of records labelled positive that the model actually found:
19: The F1 score considers Precision and Recall together; a high F1 usually means the model struck a good balance between them.
22: Accuracy, Precision, Recall and F1 can express the model's overall quality as one number, but if you want to know which classes the model tends to confuse you need a confusion matrix. It compares each test record's true class with the predicted class, counts the predictions between classes and arranges the result as a matrix.
23: For example, the test set contains three classes — network fault, hardware fault and software fault — and the model's predictions are counted as follows:
35: Each row is the true class and each column the predicted class. The numbers on the diagonal are correct predictions: for example, of 50 network-fault records, 45 were identified correctly. Numbers off the diagonal are mistakes: for example, 6 software faults were wrongly predicted as network faults. The confusion matrix shows not only how many records were right but also which classes are easily confused. In the result above, software faults being mispredicted as network faults is relatively frequent, which suggests room to improve the model's ability to tell those two classes apart. Analysing these easily confused classes reveals problems and guides further training data and model optimisation.
37: For named entity recognition, field extraction and structured information extraction, the common metrics are field accuracy and entity-level Precision, Recall and F1. They look at different granularities, so choose according to the task.
39: Field accuracy mainly measures whether the model extracts a given field correctly; it is computed as:
40: \(\text{Field accuracy} = \frac{\text{Number of correctly extracted fields}} {\text{Total number of fields to extract}} \)
41: For a task with several fields you can compute accuracy per field. For example, compute the accuracy of company names and of person names separately, to see which fields the model handles more weakly. That method has a flaw, though: it cannot tell which entities the model missed. So for extraction tasks with many entities you also need entity-level Precision, Recall and F1 for a finer evaluation.
43: For named entity recognition (NER), entity-level Precision, Recall and F1 are used; this part is similar to the classification metrics in the previous section.
45: TP (True Positive): an entity the model identified correctly;
46: FP (False Positive): the model identified an entity but got it wrong;
47: FN (False Negative): an entity exists in the reference answer but the model did not find it.
48: Precision measures how many of the entities the model found are correct:
50: Recall measures how many of the entities in the reference answer the model found:
52: F1 considers Precision and Recall together:
54: High Precision means the entities the model found are accurate overall; high Recall means it missed few; F1 measures both together.
56: Unlike classification and information extraction, what a large language model generates is usually quite open-ended and there is no single correct answer, so such tasks are evaluated on several dimensions: correctness, completeness, relevance, format adherence and hallucination.
58: Correctness mainly judges whether the generated content is right, including facts, conclusions and reasoning results. For a fine-tuned model, even fluent, well-formatted answers cannot count as good if they contain wrong facts or conclusions. Correctness is usually the most basic requirement for a generation result.
60: Completeness mainly judges whether the model answered the question fully, or omitted important information it should have included. Some answers contain no obvious error but cover only part of the question, missing key content. In that case the answer is somewhat correct but not complete. Completeness is not only about whether the answer is right but whether everything that should be answered was answered.
62: Relevance mainly judges whether the generated content stays on the user's question. A large language model sometimes generates a lot of plausible content that has little to do with the question. That content may not be wrong, but it lowers the answer's usefulness. A relevant answer should address the question directly and keep irrelevant, repeated or over-extended content to a minimum.
64: In practice, besides the content itself, the model often has to output in a specified format. For example, it may be required to return results as JSON, or to organise content in a given field order and structure. Format adherence mainly evaluates whether the model generates content per the given output requirement. Even correct content can break later programs if it is not output in the required format. For instruction-tuned models or those with fixed output requirements, format adherence is an important dimension too.
66: Hallucination means the model has generated content that lacks grounds, contradicts the facts or is simply invented. When the model does not know something, instead of saying the information is insufficient it produces a plausible fact that does not actually exist: that is a typical hallucination.
67: Hallucination is related to correctness but the focus differs. Correctness cares whether the answer is right; hallucination cares more about whether the model produced information without reliable grounds. For knowledge Q&A and similar scenarios that demand factual reliability, the model's hallucination behaviour matters especially.
69: Speech recognition (ASR) is usually evaluated on two aspects: recognition accuracy and processing efficiency. CER and WER measure the errors in the recognition result, and RTF measures how fast the model processes speech.
70: Before introducing CER and WER, here are the symbols commonly used in speech-recognition error rates:
71: S (Substitution): an error where a correct character or word is recognised as something else;
72: D (Deletion): an error where a character or word that should have been recognised is missing;
73: I (Insertion): an error where a character or word not present in the text is added;
74: N: the total number of characters or words in the reference text.
75: CER and WER are both computed from these errors; the main difference is the unit they count in.

89: The smaller the RTF, the faster the model. An RTF below 1 means the model processes faster than the audio actually plays, which is the basic condition for real-time processing.
90: Besides CER, WER and RTF, you can also evaluate the model under different test conditions. For example, compute CER or WER under background noise, different accents, far-field recording and multiple speakers, and compare the error rates across scenarios to assess the model's recognition ability and stability in complex environments.
92: Text-to-speech (TTS) aims to turn input text into natural, clear speech. Unlike text generation, a TTS model must not only keep the generated content consistent with the input text but also care about naturalness, voice timbre and generation speed. TTS models are usually evaluated on content accuracy, speech naturalness, speaker similarity and inference performance.
94: TTS first has to read the input text correctly, avoiding mispronunciation, omissions or repetitions. For evaluation you can use an ASR model to re-recognise the TTS output as text and compare it with the original input. The content-accuracy metrics are the same as in the ASR section above: character error rate (CER) and word error rate (WER).
96: Besides reading the text correctly, TTS output needs good naturalness: whether the pace is reasonable, the pauses natural, the intonation fluent, and whether there is an obvious mechanical feel. The Mean Opinion Score (MOS) is usually used. Several testers listen to the generated speech and score it against a standard, usually on a 1-5 scale where 1 means poor quality and 5 means natural, fluent and close to a real person.

100: MOS reflects how users really hear the generated speech fairly directly, but relying on human listening makes it costly and somewhat subjective.
102: For voice cloning, multi-speaker or zero-shot TTS models, naturalness alone is not enough: the generated speech must also preserve the target speaker's timbre. A common method is to use a speaker-recognition model to extract the speaker embedding of the reference speech and of the generated speech, then compute the cosine similarity between the two vectors:
104: Where \(\mathbf{e}{ref}\) is the speaker vector of the reference speech and \(\mathbf{e}{gen}\) the speaker vector of the generated speech.
105: The higher the SIM, the closer the generated speech is to the reference speaker in timbre. This metric suits evaluating voice-cloning models especially well.
107: On inference performance TTS is similar to speech recognition: real-time factor (RTF) measures processing efficiency. The difference is that in ASR the RTF is recognition time over input audio duration, whereas in TTS it is generation time over generated audio duration. The lower the RTF, the more efficient the speech generation.
110: Where \(T_{infer}\) is the inference time needed to generate the speech and \(T_{audio}\) the duration of the generated speech.
111: For streaming TTS models you can also look at the Time to First Audio: the time from the model receiving the text request to outputting the first playable audio. The lower it is, the sooner the user hears speech, which matters especially for real-time voice interaction.
113: For text-to-image, image-to-image and image editing, a single metric can hardly capture the result fully. Text-to-image needs to judge whether the generated image matches the text description; image editing also needs to judge whether the result preserves the subject and structure of the original; and assessing a model's overall quality also involves image quality and realism.
115: For text-to-image the first thing to judge is whether the generated image matches the input description. If the prompt requires a specific subject, scene or style, the generated image should contain them as far as possible.
116: A common approach is to use a vision-language model such as CLIP to map text and image into the same feature space and compute their similarity. CLIP was proposed by Radford et al. in 2021 and trained on large-scale image-text data, letting the model learn the correspondence between image content and natural language. The cosine similarity of image and text can be written as:
120: For image-to-image and image editing there is usually also an original or reference image. Such tasks must judge not only whether the result meets the text requirement but whether the important content of the original was preserved.
121: In product-image editing, for example, you may change the background, lighting or overall style while wanting the product itself, its structure and its logo to stay consistent. Here you can evaluate the edit by comparing the generated image with the reference image.
122: SSIM (Structural Similarity Index) is a classic full-reference image-quality method proposed by Wang et al. in 2004. It compares two images on luminance, contrast and structure, paying particular attention to whether the structural information changed.
123: Besides SSIM you can use LPIPS (Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity) to measure the perceptual difference between two images. LPIPS uses a deep neural network to extract image features and judges the perceptual difference from the distance between features. Research shows deep features reflect human perception of image similarity fairly well. SSIM and LPIPS both need a reference image but look at different angles: SSIM focuses more on structural change and LPIPS more on perceptual difference. In practice choose the metric that fits the editing goal.
124: For tasks with a reference image, such as image editing and image-to-image, you can compute the similarity between the generated image and the reference image.
126: The metrics above mainly compare one generated image with text or a reference image. To evaluate a model's overall generation quality you usually need a statistical analysis over a batch of generated images.
127: FID (Fréchet Inception Distance) was proposed by Heusel et al. in 2017 and mainly measures the difference in feature distribution between generated and real images, FID. FID first uses an image model to extract features from real and generated images, then estimates the distribution of each set and computes the distance between the two distributions. FID compares not two specific images but two batches in feature distribution. The lower the FID, the closer the generated distribution is to the real one, which suits comparing models overall.
131: Besides judging whether an image matches the description, you can also evaluate generated images automatically from a visual quality angle. Aesthetic score usually uses data containing human aesthetic ratings or preferences to train an evaluation model, letting it learn people's preference for visual quality, and then scores generated images automatically.
132: Such methods usually reflect composition, colour, lighting, sharpness and overall visual appeal together. A higher score generally means better visual performance under that evaluation model. Aesthetic evaluation is somewhat subjective, and different scoring models may have different training data and tastes, so aesthetic score is better as a supporting metric and cannot represent image generation quality on its own.
134: Objective metrics can assess the result in terms of text-image consistency, image similarity and feature distribution, but they do not fully reflect how an image actually looks. So image generation tasks usually also need human evaluation, judging quality from human visual perception and real usage needs.
135: Human evaluation can focus on the following:
136: Content consistency: whether the generated image matches the input description or editing requirement;
137: Visual quality: whether the image is clear and natural, and whether there is obvious distortion, blur or structural error;
138: Subject consistency: for image-to-image and editing, whether the main objects such as people or products stay consistent with the reference image;
139: Detail quality: whether error-prone areas such as hands, text, logos and edges are normal;
140: Practical usability: whether the result can be used directly in real business scenarios such as posters or product displays.
141: To reduce differences from personal judgement, you can set a uniform scoring standard in advance and have several raters evaluate separately. Subjective evaluation finds visual problems that automatic metrics miss, so image-generation evaluation usually combines objective metrics with subjective evaluation to judge a model's output more fully.
143: A video generation model produces continuous video from inputs such as text or images. Compared with image generation, video must keep not only single-frame quality but the continuity between frames, the plausibility of motion and the consistency between the generated content and the input conditions. So video models are usually evaluated on text-video consistency, overall video quality, temporal consistency, motion quality and subjective viewing.
145: Like text-to-image, text-to-video must evaluate the semantic consistency between the generated content and the input text. The difference is that video consists of consecutive frames, so the match between the whole video content and the description matters. A common method is to sample several frames from the generated video, compute each frame's semantic similarity with the input text using a vision-language model such as CLIP, and average over the frames (often called the Frame-average CLIP Score):
147: Where \(N\) is the number of frames evaluated, \(\mathbf{v}_{\text{frame}_i}\) is the feature vector of frame \(i\), \(\mathbf{v}_{\text{text}}\) is the feature vector of the input text, and \(\operatorname{Similarity}(\cdot, \cdot)\) is cosine similarity. The higher the score, the better the video content matches the text semantically. This metric mainly covers static spatial content, so it cannot fully reflect motion coherence and physical temporal logic; it should be combined with temporal consistency and motion quality.
149: Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) is the core metric for generation-distribution quality in video generation, measuring the difference in deep feature distribution between a set of generated videos and a set of real videos. To compute FVD you first extract deep features from the real and generated videos, estimate the Gaussian parameters (mean and covariance) of each set and compute their Fréchet distance: \(\mathrm{FVD} = \|\mu_r - \mu_g\|_2^2 + \operatorname{Tr}\left(\Sigma_r + \Sigma_g - 2\left(\Sigma_r^{1/2} \Sigma_g \Sigma_r^{1/2}\right)^{1/2}\right)\)
150: Where \(\mu_r\) and \(\Sigma_r\) are the mean vector and covariance of the real video features, \(\mu_g\) and \(\Sigma_g\) those of the generated video features, and \(\operatorname{Tr}(\cdot)\) the trace of a matrix. A lower FVD means the generated distribution is closer to the real one, indicating better combined visual fidelity, temporal plausibility and sample diversity.
152: Temporal consistency evaluates how stable the generated video is over time. A video consists of consecutive frames, which must not only each look good but transition smoothly in subject appearance, background texture, colour and style. In a character scene, for example, if facial features or clothing texture flicker or distort between frames, the viewing experience suffers badly however good single frames look. In practice a common method is to extract representations of consecutive frames with an image feature network and compute the mean cosine similarity of adjacent frames. 154: Where \(\mathbf{f}_i\) and \(\mathbf{f}_{i+1}\) are the visual feature vectors of frames \(i\) and \(i+1\), and \(N\) is the number of sampled frames. Usually a higher \(TC\) means smaller visual jumps between frames and a more stable picture. Temporal consistency is not simply better the higher it is: when a model degenerates and generates an almost static image, \(TC\) is abnormally high. It must be judged together with dynamic degree and motion amplitude.
156: A video generation model must not only avoid flicker but keep the subject's motion trajectory coherent and natural, avoiding sudden limb changes or instant displacement that defies physics. Motion smoothness measures how smoothly motion speed and acceleration change over time. In practice it usually relies on a pre-trained optical-flow model such as RAFT to extract dense optical flow or motion vectors between adjacent frames. Let the motion vector (or average optical flow) from frame \(t\) to frame \(t+1\) be \(\mathbf{v}_t\); the motion change error \(E_{\text{motion}}\) can be defined from the difference between motion vectors of adjacent intervals:
158: Where \(\mathbf{v}_t\) reflects the motion state at stage \(t\); the smaller \(E_{\text{motion}}\), the fewer sudden changes in acceleration and the smoother the motion.
160: Because a single metric can hardly reflect a video generation model's ability fully, a comprehensive framework such as VBench can be used for multi-dimensional evaluation. VBench splits video generation quality into several dimensions, such as subject consistency, background consistency, motion smoothness, dynamic degree, aesthetic quality and imaging quality. Compared with single metrics such as CLIP Score and FVD, VBench's advantage is analysing the result from picture quality, temporal stability, motion and condition consistency, which suits comparing video generation models overall.
162: The output of a large language model is fairly open, and the same question often has several reasonable answers. Automatic metrics alone can hardly judge whether an answer is correct and fits the user's needs, so human evaluation remains important when assessing a fine-tuned model. For open-ended content that automatic metrics cannot judge accurately, blind tests or multi-rater scoring can be used. Raters can judge the model's output on correctness, completeness, relevance, instruction following, expression quality and safety.
163: In practice you can set a uniform scoring standard in advance, for example scoring each dimension from 1 to 5. To reduce raters' preconceptions about the model, hide the model name and version and let them score by content only (a blind test). To compare a model before and after fine-tuning, you can show both answers to the same question anonymously and have raters pick the better one.
164: Because human evaluation is subjective, important evaluations can use multiple raters: the same content is evaluated independently by several raters and the scores are aggregated. When raters differ a lot, check whether the standard is clear enough, which improves consistency and reliability. Human evaluation costs more time and effort but finds problems that automatic metrics miss. When assessing a fine-tuning result, combining automatic and human evaluation judges more fully whether the model really improved.
